title: Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques
description: Master Class 11 Organic Chemistry basic principles: IUPAC nomenclature, isomerism, electronic effects, reaction mechanisms and purification techniques with solved examples and tests on GrowQR.

topics.title: Classification, Nomenclature & Isomerism
topics.concept:
Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon is special because it is tetravalent and shows catenation — its atoms join one another in long chains, branches and rings. A carbon atom with four single bonds is $sp^3$ hybridised and tetrahedral (bond angle $109.5^\circ$); with one double bond it is $sp^2$ and planar ($120^\circ$); with a triple bond it is $sp$ and linear ($180^\circ$).

Structural representations

The same molecule can be drawn three ways. The Lewis (complete) structure shows every atom and bond; the condensed formula omits some bonds (e.g. $CH_3CH_2CH_2OH$); the bond-line (skeletal) formula draws only the carbon skeleton as a zig-zag — each line-end and vertex is a carbon, and hydrogens on carbon are understood. Bond-line drawings are quick and are the working language of organic chemistry.

Classification

Compounds are first split into acyclic (open-chain) and cyclic (closed-chain). Cyclic ones are homocyclic (only carbon in the ring, e.g. benzene) or heterocyclic (a hetero-atom such as N or O in the ring, e.g. pyridine). A functional group is the reactive atom or group that decides chemical behaviour — $−OH$ (alcohol), $−CHO$ (aldehyde), $−COOH$ (carboxylic acid), $−NH_2$ (amine), and so on. A homologous series is a family with the same functional group and a constant difference of $CH_2$ (14 u) between successive members; they share a general formula and graded physical properties.

IUPAC nomenclature

A name has three parts: root word (chain length: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-…), a suffix for the principal functional group (-ane, -ene, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid) and a prefix for substituents (methyl-, chloro-, nitro-). Steps: pick the longest chain containing the functional group; number it so the principal group gets the lowest locant; name and number substituents alphabetically; combine. Thus $CH_3CH(CH_3)CH_2OH$ is 2-methylpropan-1-ol.

Isomerism

Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Structural (constitutional) isomers differ in connectivity: chain, position, functional-group and metamerism. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different 3-D arrangement — geometrical (cis–trans) from restricted rotation about a double bond, and optical from a chiral carbon (four different groups), giving non-superimposable mirror images.

examples.solution:
1. Expand: a chain $CH_3−CH(CH_3)−CH_2−CH_3$.
  2. The longest chain has 4 carbons → root but, all single bonds → butane.
  3. Number from the end giving the methyl branch the lowest locant: the $CH_3$ branch is on C-2.

Answer: 2-methylbutane.

examples.problem: Write the bond-line formula meaning of a zig-zag with five vertices and a terminal $−COOH$, then name it.
examples.solution:
1. Five carbons in the chain including the $−COOH$ carbon → root pent.
  2. The principal group is carboxylic acid → suffix -oic acid; its carbon is C-1.
  3. No other substituents, so the name is pentanoic acid, $CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2COOH$.

Answer: Pentanoic acid ($C_4H_9COOH$).

examples.problem: Draw and name all the chain isomers of $C_5H_{12}$.
examples.solution:
1. Straight chain: $CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3$ → pentane.
  2. One branch: $(CH_3)_2CHCH_2CH_3$ → 2-methylbutane.
  3. Two branches on one carbon: $C(CH_3)_4$ → 2,2-dimethylpropane.

Answer: Three chain isomers: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane.

examples.problem: Identify the type of isomerism between $CH_3OCH_3$ and $CH_3CH_2OH$.
examples.solution:
1. Both have molecular formula $C_2H_6O$.
  2. $CH_3OCH_3$ is an ether; $CH_3CH_2OH$ is an alcohol — different functional groups.
  3. Same formula, different functional group → functional isomerism.

Answer: Functional (group) isomerism.

examples.problem: Does but-2-ene show geometrical isomerism? Explain.
examples.solution:
1. Structure: $CH_3−CH=CH−CH_3$; the double bond restricts rotation.
  2. Each doubly-bonded carbon carries an $H$ and a $CH_3$ — two different groups each.
  3. So the two $CH_3$ can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans).

Answer: Yes — it exists as cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene.

examples.problem: Why does butan-2-ol show optical isomerism but butan-1-ol does not?
examples.solution:
1. Optical isomerism needs a chiral (asymmetric) carbon bonded to four different groups.
  2. In butan-2-ol C-2 bears $−H$, $−OH$, $−CH_3$ and $−CH_2CH_3$ — all different.
  3. In butan-1-ol the $−CH_2OH$ carbon has two $H$ atoms, so no carbon has four different groups.

Answer: Butan-2-ol has a chiral carbon (C-2) and is optically active; butan-1-ol has none.

recap: Carbon is tetravalent and catenates; hybridisation sets shape — $sp^3$ tetrahedral ($109.5^\circ$), $sp^2$ planar ($120^\circ$), $sp$ linear ($180^\circ$).
Structures can be written as Lewis, condensed or bond-line formulae; in bond-line every vertex/end is a carbon with H understood.
A functional group decides reactivity; a homologous series shares a functional group with a constant $CH_2$ (14 u) difference.
IUPAC name = prefix (substituents) + root (longest chain) + suffix (principal group), numbered to give the principal group the lowest locant.
Structural isomers (chain, position, functional, metamerism) differ in connectivity; stereoisomers (geometrical, optical) differ only in 3-D arrangement.

quiz.q: The hybridisation and shape at a carbon forming a triple bond is:
quiz.explanation: A triple bond means one $sigma$ + two $pi$; the carbon uses $sp$ hybrids and is linear ($180^\circ$).
Longest chain through the $−OH$ carbon is 3 C (propan-1-ol) with two methyls on C-2: 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol.
Both are $C_4H_{10}$ but differ in carbon-skeleton (straight vs branched) — chain isomerism.

quiz.q: Which compound can exhibit cis–trans (geometrical) isomerism?
quiz.explanation: Each doubly bonded carbon in but-2-ene carries two different groups (H and CH$_3$), so cis and trans forms exist.

topics.title: Electronic Effects & Reaction Mechanisms
topics.concept:
Reactions begin with the breaking of a covalent bond. Homolytic fission splits a bond so each atom keeps one electron, giving neutral free radicals ($A−B \rightarrow A^{\bullet}+B^{\bullet}$); it is favoured in non-polar media and by heat or light. Heterolytic fission splits a bond so one atom takes both electrons, giving ions — a carbocation (positive carbon, electron-deficient) or a carbanion (negative carbon, electron-rich).

Nucleophiles and electrophiles

A nucleophile ('nucleus-loving') is electron-rich and donates a lone/bonding pair — $OH^-$, $CN^-$, $NH_3$, $H_2O$. An electrophile ('electron-loving') is electron-deficient and accepts a pair — $H^+$, $NO_2^+$, $BF_3$, $Cl^+$. Curved arrows in a mechanism always show movement from the electron-rich site to the electron-poor site.

Electronic displacement effects

  • Inductive effect (I): permanent polarisation of a $sigma$-bond by an electronegative atom, transmitted through the chain and falling off with distance. Electron-withdrawing groups ($−NO_2$, $−Cl$) show $−I$; alkyl groups show $+I$ (electron-releasing).
  • Resonance / mesomeric effect (M): delocalisation of $pi$/lone-pair electrons over a conjugated system, shown by resonance structures and a resonance hybrid. It stabilises ions (e.g. the carboxylate $RCOO^-$) and is stronger than the inductive effect.
  • Electromeric effect (E): a temporary, complete shift of a $pi$-pair to one atom in the presence of an attacking reagent; it disappears when the reagent is removed.
  • Hyperconjugation: delocalisation of $sigma(C−H)$ electrons of an alkyl group into an adjacent empty $p$ or $pi$ orbital ('no-bond resonance'). More $\alpha$-hydrogens means more hyperconjugation and greater stability.

Stability of carbocations

Carbocations are stabilised by $+I$ and by hyperconjugation, so the order is $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > CH_3^+$. The same factors make the order of free-radical stability run $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$.

Types of organic reactions

Substitution — one atom/group replaces another (e.g. $CH_4+Cl_2 \rightarrow CH_3Cl+HCl$). Addition — reagent adds across a multiple bond (e.g. $CH_2=CH_2+H_2 \rightarrow CH_3CH_3$). Elimination — a small molecule is removed to form a multiple bond (dehydration of an alcohol). Rearrangement — atoms/groups migrate within a molecule (e.g. $1^\circ \rightarrow 2^\circ$ carbocation shift).

examples.problem: Classify the fission and product in (i) $Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2Cl^{\bullet}$ and (ii) $CH_3Br \rightarrow CH_3^+ + Br^-$.
examples.solution:
1. (i) Each Cl keeps one electron → equal split → homolytic fission giving free radicals.
  2. (ii) Br takes both bonding electrons → unequal split → heterolytic fission.
  3. This gives a methyl carbocation $CH_3^+$ and a bromide ion $Br^-$.

Answer: (i) homolytic (free radicals); (ii) heterolytic (carbocation + anion).

examples.problem: Classify each species as nucleophile or electrophile: $OH^-$, $NO_2^+$, $NH_3$, $BF_3$.
examples.solution:
1. Nucleophiles are electron-rich, donate a pair: $OH^-$ and $NH_3$ (lone pair).
  2. Electrophiles are electron-deficient, accept a pair: $NO_2^+$ (positive) and $BF_3$ (incomplete octet on B).

Answer: Nucleophiles: $OH^-$, $NH_3$; Electrophiles: $NO_2^+$, $BF_3$.

examples.problem: Arrange the carbocations $CH_3^+$, $CH_3CH_2^+$, $(CH_3)_2CH^+$, $(CH_3)_3C^+$ in increasing order of stability.
examples.solution:
1. Stability rises with $+I$ of alkyl groups and number of $\alpha$-hydrogens (hyperconjugation).
  2. Methyl has none, $1^\circ$ ethyl a little, $2^\circ$ isopropyl more, $3^\circ$ tert-butyl most.
  3. So the order increases from methyl to tertiary.

Answer: $CH_3^+ < CH_3CH_2^+ < (CH_3)_2CH^+ < (CH_3)_3C^+$.

examples.problem: Explain, using resonance, why the carboxylate ion $CH_3COO^-$ is more stable than the ethoxide ion $CH_3CH_2O^-$.
examples.solution:
1. In $CH_3COO^-$ the negative charge is delocalised over two equivalent oxygen atoms by resonance.
  2. This spreads the charge, lowering energy and giving a stable resonance hybrid.
  3. In ethoxide the charge is localised on one oxygen with no such delocalisation.

Answer: Resonance delocalisation over two oxygens stabilises carboxylate; ethoxide has a localised charge, so it is less stable.

examples.problem: Identify the reaction type: (i) $CH_4 + Cl_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} CH_3Cl + HCl$; (ii) $CH_2=CH_2 + Br_2 \rightarrow CH_2BrCH_2Br$.
examples.solution:
1. (i) A H atom of methane is replaced by Cl — one group swaps for another.
  2. That is a substitution reaction (free-radical).
  3. (ii) $Br_2$ adds across the C=C double bond with no atom lost → addition reaction.

Answer: (i) substitution; (ii) addition.

examples.problem: Compare the inductive ($+I$) and hyperconjugative contributions of $−CH_3$ versus $−CCl_3$ on an attached carbocation.
examples.solution:
1. $−CH_3$ is electron-releasing ($+I$) and has three $\alpha$-C−H bonds for hyperconjugation → it stabilises a carbocation.
  2. $−CCl_3$ has highly electronegative chlorines, so it is electron-withdrawing ($−I$) and has no $\alpha$-C−H for hyperconjugation.
  3. Hence $−CCl_3$ destabilises an adjacent carbocation.

Answer: $−CH_3$ stabilises (+I + hyperconjugation); $−CCl_3$ destabilises (−I, no hyperconjugation).

recap: Homolytic fission gives free radicals (equal split); heterolytic fission gives ions — carbocations or carbanions.
Nucleophiles are electron-rich donors ($OH^-$, $CN^-$, $NH_3$); electrophiles are electron-deficient acceptors ($H^+$, $NO_2^+$, $BF_3$).

Inductive (+I/−I) is a permanent $sigma$ effect through bonds; resonance (mesomeric) delocalises $pi$/lone pairs; electromeric is a temporary $pi$ shift; hyperconjugation delocalises $sigma(C−H)$ electrons.
Carbocation and free-radical stability follow $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ >$ methyl, due to +I and hyperconjugation.
Organic reactions are substitution, addition, elimination or rearrangement.

quiz.q: Homolytic fission of a covalent bond produces:
quiz.explanation: Homolytic fission splits the bond equally — each atom keeps one electron, giving two neutral free radicals.

quiz.q: Which of the following acts as an electrophile?
quiz.explanation: $NO_2^+$ is electron-deficient and accepts an electron pair, so it is an electrophile; the others are nucleophiles.

quiz.q: The most stable carbocation among the following is:
quiz.explanation: The tertiary carbocation $(CH_3)_3C^+$ is most stabilised by +I and the greatest hyperconjugation.

quiz.q: Delocalisation of $\sigma(C−H)$ electrons into an adjacent empty orbital is called:
quiz.explanation: Hyperconjugation (no-bond resonance) is the delocalisation of $\sigma$ C−H electrons into an adjacent $p$ or $\pi$ orbital.

topics.title: Purification & Analysis
topics.concept:
Organic compounds prepared in the laboratory are rarely pure. The method of purification is chosen from the differences in physical properties — solubility, volatility, adsorption — between the compound and its impurities.

Methods of purification

  • Crystallisation: the most common method for solids. The compound is dissolved in a hot solvent in which it is sparingly soluble when cold; on cooling, pure crystals separate while soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor.
  • Sublimation: for solids that pass directly from solid to vapour on heating (e.g. naphthalene, camphor, benzoic acid), separating them from non-sublimable impurities.
  • Distillation: separates a volatile liquid from a non-volatile impurity, or two liquids with a large boiling-point gap. Fractional distillation separates liquids with close boiling points using a fractionating column. Distillation under reduced pressure purifies liquids that decompose at their normal boiling point (e.g. glycerol). Steam distillation purifies compounds that are steam-volatile and immiscible with water (e.g. aniline) below $100^\circ$C.
  • Differential extraction: shakes an aqueous solution with an immiscible organic solvent in which the compound is more soluble, so it transfers to the organic layer.
  • Chromatography: separates a mixture by differential adsorption/partition between a stationary and a moving phase — adsorption (column, TLC) and partition (paper) types.

Qualitative analysis — detecting elements

Carbon and hydrogen are detected by heating the compound with dry CuO: carbon gives $CO_2$ (turns lime-water milky) and hydrogen gives $H_2O$ (turns anhydrous $CuSO_4$ blue). N, S and halogens are covalently bound and are first converted to ionisable forms by Lassaigne's test: the compound is fused with sodium, forming $NaCN$, $Na_2S$, $NaX$ (and $NaSCN$). The fused extract is tested — nitrogen gives Prussian-blue $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$, sulphur gives a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside, and halogens give silver-halide precipitates with $AgNO_3$.

Quantitative estimation

  • Carbon & hydrogen (Liebig): a known mass is burnt; $CO_2$ is absorbed in KOH and $H_2O$ in anhydrous $CaCl_2$. $\%C=\dfrac{12}{44}\times\dfrac{m_{CO_2}}{m}\times100$ and $\%H=\dfrac{2}{18}\times\dfrac{m_{H_2O}}{m}\times100$.
  • Nitrogen: Dumas oxidises N to $N_2$ gas, measured over KOH; Kjeldahl converts N to $(NH_4)_2SO_4$, liberates $NH_3$ with NaOH and titrates it. $\%N=\dfrac{1.4\times N_{acid}\times V_{acid}}{m}$.
  • Halogens (Carius): heated with fuming $HNO_3$ and $AgNO_3$ to give $AgX$, weighed.
  • Sulphur: oxidised to sulphate and precipitated as $BaSO_4$.
  • Phosphorus: oxidised to phosphoric acid and precipitated as ammonium phosphomolybdate or $Mg_2P_2O_7$.

examples.problem: Which purification method would you use for (i) a mixture of camphor and salt, and (ii) glycerol that decomposes at its boiling point?
examples.solution:
1. (i) Camphor sublimes but salt does not, so heating separates the camphor as vapour.
  2. That is sublimation.
  3. (ii) Glycerol decomposes at its normal boiling point, so lower the boiling point by reducing pressure.

Answer: (i) sublimation; (ii) distillation under reduced pressure.

examples.problem: In Lassaigne's test, what observation confirms the presence of nitrogen and why is sodium fusion needed?
examples.solution:
1. Covalently bound N must be converted to an ionic form; fusion with Na gives $NaCN$.
  2. The extract with $FeSO_4$ and then $Fe^{3+}$ forms sodium hexacyanoferrate, then ferric ferrocyanide.
  3. A Prussian-blue colour or precipitate $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$ confirms nitrogen.

Answer: A Prussian-blue colour confirms N; sodium fusion converts covalent N into ionisable $CN^-$.

examples.problem: On combustion, $0.20\ \text{g}$ of an organic compound gave $0.44\ \text{g}$ of $CO_2$. Calculate the percentage of carbon.
In a Kjeldahl estimation, $0.50\ \text{g}$ of a compound liberated $NH_3$ which neutralised $25\ \text{mL}$ of $0.5\ \text{N}$ acid. Find the percentage of nitrogen.
examples.solution:
1. Use $\%N=\dfrac{1.4\times N_{acid}\times V_{acid}}{m}$ with $V$ in mL.
  2. $=\dfrac{1.4\times 0.5\times 25}{0.50}$.
  3. $=\dfrac{17.5}{0.50}=35$.

Answer: $\%N=35\%$.

examples.problem: Name the method to estimate nitrogen that works for ALL nitrogen-containing compounds, and one limitation of the alternative.
examples.solution:
1. Dumas method oxidises nitrogen of any organic compound to $N_2$ gas, so it is general.
  2. Kjeldahl converts N to ammonium sulphate, but only if N can be reduced to $−3$.
  3. Kjeldahl fails for N in rings (pyridine), $−NO_2$ and azo ($−N=N−$) groups.

Answer: Dumas is general; Kjeldahl does not work for nitro, azo or ring nitrogen.

examples.problem: Which technique separates a small amount of a coloured plant pigment mixture, and on what principle?
examples.solution:
1. Small mixtures with components of differing affinities are best resolved by chromatography.
  2. Components move at different rates between a stationary phase and a moving solvent.
  3. This works by differential adsorption (or partition) of the components.

Answer: Chromatography, based on differential adsorption/partition between stationary and mobile phases.

recap: Purification methods exploit physical differences: crystallisation (solubility), sublimation (solid→vapour), distillation/fractional/reduced-pressure/steam (volatility), extraction (solvent partition), chromatography (adsorption/partition).
Carbon gives $CO_2$ (lime-water milky) and hydrogen gives $H_2O$ (blue with anhydrous $CuSO_4$) on heating with CuO.
Lassaigne's sodium fusion converts covalent N, S, X to ionic $CN^-$, $S^{2-}$, $X^-$: N gives Prussian blue, S a violet nitroprusside colour, X a silver-halide precipitate.
Nitrogen by Dumas (as $N_2$) or Kjeldahl ($\%N=\dfrac{1.4\,N_{acid}V_{acid}}{m}$); halogens by Carius (AgX), sulphur as $BaSO_4$, phosphorus as $Mg_2P_2O_7$.

quiz.q: Glycerol, which decomposes at its normal boiling point, is best purified by:
quiz.explanation: Lowering the pressure lowers the boiling point, so glycerol distils without decomposing.

quiz.q: In Lassaigne's test, a Prussian-blue colour confirms the element:
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen (as $CN^-$ after fusion) forms ferric ferrocyanide, $Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3$, which is Prussian blue.

quiz.q: On combustion $0.30\ \text{g}$ of a compound gave $0.22\ \text{g}$ of $CO_2$. The percentage of carbon is:
The Kjeldahl method CANNOT be used to estimate nitrogen present as:
quiz.explanation: Kjeldahl fails for nitro, azo and ring nitrogen because such N cannot be converted to ammonium sulphate.

online.title: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles — Online Test

questions.q: The shape around an $sp^2$ hybridised carbon is:
questions.explanation: $sp^2$ carbon (one double bond) is trigonal planar with $120^\circ$ bond angles.

questions.q: In a bond-line (skeletal) formula, each line-end and vertex represents:
questions.explanation: Vertices and ends are carbons; the attached hydrogens are understood.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of $(CH_3)_2CHCH_2CH_3$ is:
questions.explanation: Longest chain is 4 C (butane) with a methyl on C-2: 2-methylbutane.

questions.q: Ethanol and dimethyl ether ($C_2H_6O$) are:
questions.explanation: They have the same formula but different functional groups (alcohol vs ether) — functional isomerism.

questions.q: Which molecule shows geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism?
questions.explanation: Each doubly bonded carbon of but-2-ene bears two different groups, giving cis and trans forms.

questions.q: Successive members of a homologous series differ in molar mass by:
questions.explanation: They differ by a $CH_2$ unit, which is $12+2=14$ u.

questions.q: Heterolytic fission of $CH_3−Br$ most readily gives:
questions.explanation: Bromine, being more electronegative, takes both electrons, giving $CH_3^+$ and $Br^-$.

questions.q: Which of the following is a nucleophile?
questions.explanation: $CN^-$ is electron-rich and donates a lone pair, so it is a nucleophile.

questions.q: The correct order of carbocation stability is:
questions.explanation: Tertiary cations are most stabilised by +I and hyperconjugation: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > CH_3^+$.

questions.q: The $−NO_2$ group exerts which inductive effect?
questions.explanation: Nitro is strongly electron-withdrawing, so it shows a $−I$ effect.

questions.q: Hyperconjugation involves delocalisation of electrons from:
options: a lone pair into a $\sigma$ bond
questions.explanation: Hyperconjugation is 'no-bond resonance' — $\sigma(C−H)$ electrons delocalise into an adjacent empty $p$ or $\pi$ orbital.

questions.q: Dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide to an alkene is a reaction of type:
questions.explanation: A small molecule (HX) is removed and a double bond forms — an elimination reaction.

questions.q: The carboxylate ion $RCOO^-$ is stabilised mainly by:
questions.explanation: Its negative charge is delocalised equally over two oxygens by resonance.

questions.q: Camphor is best purified by:
questions.explanation: Camphor sublimes (solid → vapour) on heating, so sublimation separates it from non-sublimable impurities.

questions.q: In Lassaigne's test, halogens are confirmed by a precipitate with:
questions.explanation: $X^-$ ions give silver-halide precipitates with $AgNO_3$ (AgCl white, AgBr pale yellow, AgI yellow).

questions.q: On combustion $0.25\ \text{g}$ of a compound gave $0.44\ \text{g}$ $CO_2$. The $\%C$ is:
Nitrogen present as a nitro ($−NO_2$) group is best estimated by the:
questions.explanation: Kjeldahl fails for nitro/azo/ring nitrogen; Dumas oxidises any N to $N_2$ and is general.

questions.q: Glycerol is purified by distillation under reduced pressure because it:
options: decomposes at its normal boiling point
is a gas at room temperature
questions.explanation: Lowering the pressure lowers its boiling point so it distils without decomposing.

imo.title: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles — IMO/Olympiad Test

questions.q: The number of $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds in propyne $CH_3−C{\equiv}CH$ is:
questions.explanation: C−H bonds (4) + C−C (1) + the $\sigma$ of the triple bond (1) = 6 $\sigma$; the triple bond adds 2 $\pi$.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of $CH_3CH(CH_3)CH(C_2H_5)CH_2CH_3$ is:
questions.explanation: Longest chain is 5 C (pentane); ethyl on C-3, methyl on C-2; alphabetised: 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane.

questions.q: How many structural isomers (chain + position skeleton) exist for $C_4H_9Cl$?
questions.explanation: 1-chloro-, 2-chlorobutane, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane — four isomers.

questions.q: Which carbocation is the MOST stable?
questions.explanation: The allyl cation is resonance-stabilised; the vinyl cation is especially unstable ($sp$ carbon).

questions.q: Among $−F$, $−Cl$, $−Br$, $−I$, the strongest $−I$ (inductive) effect is shown by:
questions.explanation: The inductive effect tracks electronegativity, which is greatest for fluorine.

questions.q: The number of $\alpha$-hydrogens available for hyperconjugation in the tert-butyl cation $(CH_3)_3C^+$ is:
questions.explanation: Three methyl groups, each with three C−H bonds, give nine $\alpha$-hydrogens.

questions.q: Which species is both a Brønsted base and a Lewis base?
questions.explanation: $NH_3$ accepts a proton (Brønsted base) and donates its lone pair (Lewis base).

questions.q: The empirical formula of a compound with $40\%$ C, $6.7\%$ H and $53.3\%$ O (by mass) is:
A Carius estimation of $0.20\ \text{g}$ of an organochlorine compound gave $0.287\ \text{g}$ of AgCl. The $\%Cl$ is about (AgCl = 143.5, Cl = 35.5):
In Kjeldahl's method, $0.25\ \text{g}$ of a compound liberated ammonia that needed $25\ \text{mL}$ of $0.25\ \text{N}$ acid. The $\%N$ is:
Which pair are metamers (same formula, different alkyl groups on the same functional group)?
questions.explanation: Methyl propyl ether and diethyl ether ($C_4H_{10}O$) differ in the alkyl groups around oxygen — metamerism.

questions.q: Steam distillation purifies a compound that is:
questions.explanation: Steam distillation works for compounds volatile in steam and immiscible with water (e.g. aniline), distilling below $100^\circ$C.
